title: Drummers, Ray Anderson's classical students and an eighth-grade pianist
summary: They discuss drummers and written licks, Ray Anderson's improvisation group and a student who clung to the music.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Oh yeah and I say man, “Don’t play any of the licks with the horns. Just give me time. Please.” Why do they write the licks in it?

Really. I know. I’m trying to remember who else said that that I interviewed, they said that about the Basie band, that that’s why they swung so much because the drummers didn’t have to nail everything.

Yeah and if you nail something, great. You know like sometimes it’s like that’s — now you might have a great drummer that does that. But don’t try to synthesize that and put it on the drum part and say every drummer has to do that now.

When you know it, when you’ve played it for two years without music, then you’ve got it. So they realize it’s many, many years, since man existed they were making music I’m sure. I was telling, cavemen, they were making “rock” music then. And so they start getting it. You do all these things and like they start just really, and sometimes I’ll like set up — oh this last one was so beautiful — just when I happened to be in the room, I’ll set up like a tenor, a bari — maybe two tenors, a bari and a trombone over here. I got them into this little group [scats] something like that. And then I’d give trumpets here, this, and make it all go together. And I’d have a soloist, like a lead alto player, this young girl, and I put her on a chair and I said, “Can you stand up? Stand up on this chair.” And she’s blowing like this. And those guys setting up this basic rhythm, they’re starting to do steps. And this is all, because they had no idea what it was going to be, they’re feeling the groove. And sometimes I don’t even have the drums play but I did this time. And it’s like afterwards, you know, it’s so intimate. When you’ve got your eye on that paper, man, it’s not very intimate. And the thing is like, classical music, forget it. I’ve actually, you know Ray Anderson, the trombone player, he teaches out at the State University at Stonybrook. And once in a while I’ll go sub for him when he’s on the road or something. And I mean he’s a dear friend. His daughter is my Goddaughter, we’ve been buddies forever, a phenomenal player. I don’t know if you’ve heard his stuff. So anyway, so he’s got a graduate group of classical musicians, two pianists, I think a bassoon player, a flute player and maybe percussion. Just learning improvisation, not necessarily jazz. But just a group improvisation. And they are so stuck on the paper. But they opened up, they were so beautiful you know. He has his techniques. Like he told me the first thing he had them do was, “Play as ugly as you can, real loud and ugly. Go guess what you think this should be.” He is great. And so I would do my stuff with them, you know get them just to breathe and make a sound, and then sometimes it goes crazy. I remember working with an eighth grade piano student who was so married to the music, this was many years ago,

at a high school in New Jersey. And I couldn’t get her at first to just like play without the music without going to something that she hadn’t memorized. So now this was actually before the cheese or anything. And I said, “Come on let’s sit on the floor.” We sat on the floor with the piano behind us, and just put one hand up there and hit one note, and act like you’ve never heard a piano in your life, it would be just like a baby hearing the first note. Bing. And after a half hour of that she just started opening up.
Whether they’re going to be an improviser or not.
